zh:
卷第八
隋天台智者大師說
弟子法慎記
弟子灌頂再治
釋禪波羅蜜修證第七之四（修證通明觀）
今辨此禪，大意為三：一者、釋名；二者、辨次位；三者、明修證。一、釋名者，所以此禪名為通明觀者，此觀方法出《大集》經文，無別名目。北國諸禪師修得此禪，欲以授人，既不知名字，正欲安根本禪裡，而法相逈殊。若對十六特勝，則名目全不相關；若安之背捨、勝處，觀行方法條然別異。既進退並不相應，所以諸師別作名目，名為通明觀禪。或有說言：「《華嚴經》有此名目。」
en:
Fascicle Eight
Spoken by the Great Master Zhiyi of Tiantai, of the Sui dynasty
Recorded by his disciple Fashen
Revised and edited by his disciple Guanding
Explaining Dhyāna-Pāramitā's Cultivation and Realization, Topic 7, Part 4 (Cultivating and Realizing the Thorough-and-Bright Contemplation)
Here, this dhyāna is distinguished, in its general sense, in three parts: explaining the name; distinguishing its sequence of stages; and clarifying its cultivation and realization.

First, explaining the name: as for why this dhyāna is named the thorough-and-bright contemplation, this contemplative method is given in the text of the Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra, without any separate name of its own there. The various dhyāna masters of the northern lands, having cultivated and attained this dhyāna and wishing to transmit it to others, not knowing its proper name, at first wished simply to place it among the root dhyānas — but its own dharma-characteristics differ vastly from those. Matched against the sixteen special excellences, its own terms bear no relation to them at all; placed alongside the liberations or the stations of mastery, its own contemplative method and practice differ entirely as well. Since it corresponds properly with neither, in either direction, the various masters accordingly gave it a separate name of its own, calling it the dhyāna of thorough-and-bright contemplation. Some, further, say that this very name is given in the Avataṃsaka Sūtra.

zh: 所言通者，謂從初修習即通觀三事。若觀息時，即通照色心；若觀色，乃至心亦如是。此法明淨，能開心眼，無諸暗蔽，既觀一達三，徹見無閡，故名通明。復次，善修此禪，必定能發六通、三明故。《大集經》明法行比丘修此禪時，欲得神通，即能得之。今言通者，即是能得六通；明者，即是能生三明。此因中說果，故言通明觀。
en: As for what is meant by "thorough": this means that, from the very outset of its cultivation, one thoroughly contemplates all three matters — the breath, form, and mind — together. When contemplating the breath, one thereby illuminates form and mind together as well; and when contemplating form, the same holds all the way through to mind as well. This dharma is bright and pure, able to open the mind's own eye, free of every obscuring darkness — contemplating one, all three are reached at once, seeing through them without any obstruction whatsoever — hence it is named "thorough and bright."

Furthermore: skillfully cultivating this dhyāna is certain to bring forth the six supernormal powers and the three insights. The Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra clarifies that, when the dharma-practicing monk cultivates this dhyāna, wishing to attain supernormal powers, he is thereby able to attain them directly. Here, "thorough" refers precisely to being able to attain the six supernormal powers; and "bright" refers precisely to being able to give rise to the three insights. This speaks of the result already within the cause — hence it is called the thorough-and-bright contemplation.

zh: 問曰：餘禪亦能發六通、三明，何故獨此禪說為通明？答曰：餘禪乃有發通明之義，不如此禪利疾，故名通明。問曰：如《大集經》亦有別釋此禪名義，故經言：「所言禪者，疾故名禪。疾大疾，住大住，靜寂靜，觀滅遠離，是名為禪。」今何故別立名耶？答曰：彼經雖有此釋，於義乃顯，而名猶漫，既不的有名目，故復更立通明之名。
en: Question: the other dhyānas, too, are able to bring forth the six supernormal powers and the three insights — why, then, is only this dhyāna spoken of as "thorough and bright"? Answer: the other dhyānas do indeed carry this same sense of bringing forth thoroughness and brightness, but not so swiftly and sharply as this dhyāna — hence this alone is named thorough-and-bright.

Question: the Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra itself gives a separate explanation of this dhyāna's own name and meaning, the sūtra saying: "As for what is called dhyāna: it is swift, and so is named dhyāna — swift, greatly swift; abiding, greatly abiding; still, utterly still; contemplating cessation, far removed — this is what is named dhyāna." Why, then, is a separate name established here instead? Answer: although that sūtra does give this explanation, its sense, though made clear there, still leaves the name itself somewhat diffuse — since no definite, specific name is actually given there, a further name, "thorough-and-bright," is established here instead.

The origin story here is unusually candid about how the name itself came about — not from a single scriptural source, but from northern dhyāna masters who had already cultivated this practice and needed some name for it once they discovered it fit neatly into none of the treatise's existing categories. The name is justified at two levels. First, by the method itself: any one of breath, form, or mind illuminates all three at once ("thorough"), and the dharma is bright and pure, opening the mind's own eye ("bright"). Second, by its fruit: "thorough" names the six supernormal powers and "bright" the three insights — "speaking of the result already within the cause," as the text itself puts it.

zh: 第二、明次位者，此禪無別次位，猶是約根本四禪、四空立次位。但於一一禪內更有增勝出世間觀定之法，能發無漏及三明、六通疾利，亦於非想後心滅諸心數，入滅受想定，故不同根本暗證取著，無有神智功能。是故雖復次位同於根本，而觀慧殊別，恐人謬解，故立別名。雖名有異，而次位無差。
en: Second, clarifying its sequence of stages: this dhyāna has no separate sequence of stages of its own — it, too, is established with reference to the sequence of stages of the root four dhyānas and the four formless concentrations. It is simply that, within each single dhyāna, there is, further, a superior, world-transcending dharma of contemplation and concentration present, able to bring forth the uncontaminated, along with the three insights and the six supernormal powers, swiftly and sharply — and, following neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the mind's various mental factors are extinguished, entering the concentration of the cessation of sensation and perception. Hence it differs from the root dhyānas' own dark realization and clinging attachment, which lack any such spiritual, wisdom-bearing capacity at all. Hence, although its sequence of stages is the same as the root dhyānas', its contemplative wisdom differs entirely — and, fearing this might be misunderstood, a separate name is established for it. Though the name differs, the sequence of stages itself shows no difference at all.

zh: 問曰：若此禪得入滅定，與九次第定有何異耶？答曰：修此定時，心心無間，亦得說為九次第定，然終非是具足九次第定法。是事在下自當可見。若比准《成實論》解九定、八解，亦是具足。
en: Question: if this dhyāna is able to enter the concentration of cessation, how does it differ from the nine sequential concentrations? Answer: at the time this concentration is cultivated, mind follows mind without interruption, and so it, too, may be spoken of as the nine sequential concentrations — yet, in the end, it is not the same as the nine sequential concentrations' own complete dharma. This matter will be seen for itself below. Compared against the Satyasiddhi-śāstra's own explanation of the nine concentrations and the eight liberations, it, too, is complete in this same respect.

This is a precise statement of what actually distinguishes the thorough-and-bright contemplation from the ordinary root dhyānas — not a different ladder of attainments, but the identical ladder climbed with contemplative wisdom attached at every rung, all the way to a genuine cessation of sensation and perception rather than the "dark realization and clinging attachment" of an ordinary practitioner reaching the same formal stage. The separate name exists precisely to prevent this crucial difference from being missed by someone who sees only the shared stage-sequence.

items.zh: 通明觀 · 明修證 · 修習如心

zh: 第三、明修證，此禪既無別次位，還約根本次位辨修證也。第一、先明修證初禪之相，如《大集經》說：「言初禪者，亦名為具，亦名為離。離者，謂離五蓋；具者，謂具五支。五支者，謂覺、觀、喜、安、定。云何為覺？如心覺、大覺，思惟、大思惟，觀於心性，是名為覺。云何為觀？觀心行、大行、遍行、隨意，是名為觀。云何為喜？如真實知、大知，心動至心，是名為喜。云何為安？謂心安、身安、受安，受於樂觸，是名為安。云何為定？謂心住、大住，不亂於緣，不謬，無有顛倒，是名為定。」即是彼經略釋修證通明初禪之相。推此經文所明五支，則與餘經論所明大異，故須別釋。
en: Third, clarifying its cultivation and realization: since this dhyāna has no separate sequence of stages of its own, its cultivation and realization, too, are distinguished with reference to the root dhyānas' own sequence of stages.

First, clarifying beforehand the mark of cultivating and realizing the first dhyāna, as the Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra says: "As for the first dhyāna: it is named both 'complete' and 'free.' As for 'free': this means free of the five hindrances. As for 'complete': this means complete in the five factors. The five factors are: initial thought, sustained reflection, joy, ease, and concentration. What is meant by initial thought? Suchness-thought; initial thought, great initial thought; deliberation, great deliberation; contemplating the nature of mind — this is named initial thought. What is meant by sustained reflection? Contemplating the conduct of mind, great conduct, pervasive conduct, and conduct at will — this is named sustained reflection. What is meant by joy? Suchness-knowledge, great knowledge; the mind moved all the way to the very heart of mind itself — this is named joy. What is meant by ease? This means ease of mind, ease of body, and ease of sensation, receiving a blissful touch — this is named ease. What is meant by concentration? This means the mind abiding, greatly abiding, undisturbed by any object, unmistaken, free of any inversion whatsoever — this is named concentration." This is precisely that sūtra's own brief explanation of the mark of cultivating and realizing the thorough-and-bright contemplation's first dhyāna. Reasoning through what this sūtra passage clarifies regarding the five factors, this differs vastly from what the other sūtras and treatises clarify — hence it must be explained separately here.

zh: 今先釋如心。如心者，即是初禪前方便定發也。亦即是未到地，但證不孤發，要由修習。云何修習？行者從初安心即觀於息、色、心三事俱無分別。觀三事者，必須先觀息道。云何觀息？謂攝心靜坐，調和氣息，一心諦觀息想遍身出入。若慧心明利，即覺息入無積聚，出無分散，來無所經由，去無所履涉。雖復明覺息入出遍身，如空中風，性無所有。是則略說觀息如心相。
en: Here, "suchness-thought" is first explained. Suchness-thought is precisely the preliminary expedient concentration that arises before the first dhyāna itself — it is, in fact, the "not-yet-arrived" state, though its realization does not arise on its own, in isolation, but necessarily through cultivation.

How is it cultivated? The practitioner, from the very outset of settling the mind, contemplates that the three matters of breath, form, and mind are all alike without any distinct discrimination between them. To contemplate these three matters, one must first contemplate the path of the breath. How does one contemplate the breath? By gathering the mind and sitting still, regulating and harmonizing the breath, closely contemplating single-mindedly the very conception of the breath going out and coming in throughout the body. If the wisdom-mind is bright and sharp, one perceives the in-breath as gathering nowhere, and the out-breath as scattering nowhere, coming from no particular course and going by no particular path. Although one clearly perceives the breath entering and leaving throughout the body in this way, it is like wind within empty space, its very nature having nothing at all present within it. This, in brief, describes contemplating the breath as suchness-thought.

zh: 次觀色如。行者既知息依於身，離身無息，即應諦觀身色如。此色本自不有，皆是先世妄想因緣，招感今世四大、造色圍虛空故，假名為身。一心諦觀頭等六分、三十六物及四大、四微，一一非身，四微、四大亦各非實，尚不自有，何能生六分之身、三十六物？無身色可得，爾時心無分別，即達色如。次觀心如。行者當知由有心故，則有身色、去來、動轉。若無此心，誰分別色？色因誰生？諦觀此心藉緣而有，生滅迅速，不見住處，亦無相貌，但有名字，名字亦空，即達心如。行者若不得三性別異，名為如心。
en: Next, contemplating form as suchness. The practitioner, already knowing that the breath depends upon the body, and that, apart from the body, there is no breath at all, should then closely contemplate the body's own form as suchness. This form is, in itself, originally without existence at all — it is entirely a matter of past-life deluded thought and causal conditions, drawing together the present life's own four elements and the form derived from them, which enclose empty space, and is thereby only provisionally named "body." Closely contemplating, single-mindedly, the six parts such as the head and the rest, the thirty-six substances, the four elements, and the four subtle elements, none of these, one by one, is itself the "body" — and even the four subtle elements and the four elements themselves are, each in turn, not truly real, not even existing on their own — how, then, could they possibly give rise to a six-part body, or to the thirty-six substances? No bodily form whatsoever can be found — at this point, the mind is free of any discrimination, and thus penetrates form as suchness.

Next, contemplating mind as suchness. The practitioner should know that it is because mind exists at all that bodily form, coming and going, movement and change, exist as well. Were this mind not present, who would discriminate form? From what would form itself arise? Closely contemplating this very mind, it, too, is found to exist only in dependence on conditions, arising and ceasing with great swiftness, no dwelling-place to be found, and no mark or appearance either — it has only a name, and even this name is itself empty — this, then, penetrates mind as suchness. The practitioner, no longer finding these three natures to be distinctly different from one another, this is named suchness-thought.

zh: 復次，行者若觀息時，既不得息，即達色、心空寂。何以故？三法不相離故。色心亦爾。若不得色心三事，即不得一切法。所以者何？由此三事和合，能生一切陰、入、界眾苦煩惱，善惡行業，往來五道，流轉不息。若了三事無生，則一切諸法本來空寂。是則略說修習如心之相。第二、明證相。此亦具有證欲界、未到地相。行者如上觀察三性，悉不可得，其心任運自住真如，其心泯然明淨，名欲界定。於此定後，心依真如法，心泯然入定，與如相應，如法持心，心定不動，泯然不見身、息、心三法異相，一往猶如虛空，故名如心，即是通明未到地也。
en: Furthermore: the practitioner, contemplating the breath, once the breath itself can no longer be found, thereby penetrates form and mind as empty and still as well. Why is this? Because these three dharmas are never actually separate from one another — and the same holds when contemplating form or mind. If these three matters, form, mind, and the rest, cannot be found, then no dharma whatsoever can be found either. Why is this? Because it is precisely through the combining together of these three matters that every aggregate, sense-base, and element, every kind of suffering and affliction, every wholesome and unwholesome karmic action, coming and going through the five realms, turning without cease, is able to arise at all. Once one understands that these three matters are themselves unarisen, then every dharma whatsoever is, in itself, originally empty and still. This, in brief, describes the mark of cultivating suchness-thought.

Second, clarifying the mark of realization: this, too, is complete with the mark of realizing both desire-realm concentration and the "not-yet-arrived" state. The practitioner, contemplating and observing these three natures as already described above, finding none of them at all, the mind now abides spontaneously, of its own accord, in true suchness itself, the mind grown indistinct, bright, and pure — this is named desire-realm concentration. Following this concentration, the mind relies on the dharma of true suchness, the mind entering concentration indistinctly, corresponding with suchness itself, the dharma of suchness sustaining the mind, the concentrated mind unmoving, indistinctly no longer seeing any distinct mark among the three dharmas of body, breath, and mind at all, altogether just like empty space — hence this is named suchness-thought, which is precisely the thorough-and-bright contemplation's own "not-yet-arrived" state.

"Suchness-thought" gives the thorough-and-bright contemplation its own distinctive starting move, distinct from every other method in this treatise: it treats all three as inseparable from the very first sitting — "these three dharmas are never actually separate from one another" — even though the contemplation itself must still begin with the path of the breath before turning to form and then mind. The regress this section runs through (form depends on mind, but searching for mind finds only something "existing only in dependence on conditions... its name itself empty") is the same reflexive move fascicle 7's own "returning" gate made against the contemplating mind — confirmation that this fascicle's method, despite its unfamiliar name, shares its deepest logic with everything already covered.

quiz.q: In distinguishing this dhyāna, into which three parts is the general sense divided?
options: explaining the name, distinguishing its stages, clarifying cultivation and realization
quiz.why: The three parts are explaining the name, distinguishing its stages, and clarifying cultivation and realization. Breath, form, and mind are what is contemplated, not the outline.

quiz.q: Where is this contemplative method found, and did it originally have a name?
options: the Lotus Sūtra, named peaceful practice
in the Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra, with no separate name
quiz.why: The method comes from the Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra, which gives it no separate name; the name was later given by the northern masters.

quiz.q: Why did the northern dhyāna masters give it a separate name?
options: it differed from the root dhyānas, bore no relation to the sixteen excellences, and differed from the liberations and stations of mastery
to match the foundations of mindfulness
quiz.why: It differed vastly from the root dhyānas, bore no relation to the special excellences, and differed from the liberations and stations of mastery, so the masters named it separately.

quiz.q: What is the first explanation of "thorough"?
options: from the outset one contemplates breath, form, and mind together; contemplating one reaches all three
quiz.why: From the very outset one contemplates the three matters together; contemplating the breath illuminates form and mind as well, so one reaches all three.

quiz.q: What is the second explanation of "thorough and bright," and why is it "the result spoken within the cause"?
options: "thorough" is attaining the six powers, "bright" giving rise to the three insights; the result names the practice
magical power and heavenly eye only
quiz.why: Skillful cultivation surely brings forth the six powers and three insights; naming the practice by them is speaking of the result within the cause.

quiz.q: Other dhyānas also bring forth the powers and insights. Why is only this one called thorough-and-bright?
options: others can, but not as swiftly and sharply
quiz.why: Other dhyānas do bring forth thoroughness and brightness, but not as swiftly and sharply as this one.

quiz.q: How does the Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra explain the word "dhyāna"?
options: swift, hence dhyāna: swift and greatly swift, abiding and greatly abiding, still and utterly still, contemplating cessation, far removed
dhyāna means a grove of merit
quiz.why: The sūtra says dhyāna is so named for being swift: swift and greatly swift, abiding and greatly abiding, still and utterly still, contemplating cessation, far removed.

quiz.q: Since the sūtra already explains the name, why establish "thorough-and-bright" separately?
options: its sense is clear but the name diffuse; lacking a definite name, a further one is established
to distinguish it from the six gates
quiz.why: The sūtra's explanation makes the sense clear, but the name remains diffuse; with no definite name, "thorough-and-bright" is established.

quiz.q: According to the Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra, when the dharma-practicing monk cultivates this dhyāna wishing for supernormal powers, what happens?
options: wishing for them, he is able to attain them
he must first practice the liberations
quiz.why: Wishing to attain supernormal powers, he is able to attain them; §14 later quotes the same sūtra on the dharma-practicing monk.

quiz.q: Does the thorough-and-bright contemplation have its own sequence of stages?
options: none; it uses the stages of the root four dhyānas and four formless concentrations
quiz.why: It has no separate stages and is established on those of the root four dhyānas and four formless concentrations.

quiz.q: If its stages are the same as the root dhyānas, why give it a separate name?
options: within each dhyāna there is world-transcending contemplation that swiftly yields the uncontaminated and the powers and leads to cessation; its wisdom differs, so a separate name prevents misunderstanding
quiz.why: Within each dhyāna there is a superior world-transcending contemplation that swiftly brings forth the uncontaminated and the powers and leads to cessation; since its wisdom differs, a separate name is given to prevent misunderstanding.

quiz.q: What fault of the root dhyānas does the thorough-and-bright contemplation avoid?
options: they exist only in the desire realm
the root dhyānas are dark realization and clinging, lacking spiritual and wisdom capacity
quiz.why: Unlike the root dhyānas' dark realization and clinging, which lack spiritual and wisdom-bearing capacity.

quiz.q: Since this dhyāna can enter cessation, how does it differ from the nine sequential concentrations?
options: mind follows mind without break, so it may be called that, but it is not the complete dharma
quiz.why: Mind follows mind without interruption, so it can be called the nine sequential concentrations, but it is not their complete dharma.

quiz.q: Compared with which treatise's account of the nine concentrations and eight liberations is it also complete?
quiz.why: Compared with the Satyasiddhi-śāstra's account of the nine concentrations and eight liberations, it is complete.

quiz.q: The sūtra calls the first dhyāna both "complete" and "free." What does each mean?
options: free of the five hindrances, complete in the five factors
free of desire realm, complete in form realm
free of self-view, complete in right view
free of sense-pleasures, complete in faculties
quiz.why: "Free" means free of the five hindrances; "complete" means complete in the five factors.

quiz.q: What five factors does the sūtra list for this first dhyāna?
options: initial thought, sustained reflection, joy, ease, concentration
quiz.why: The five are initial thought, sustained reflection, joy, ease, and concentration, using "ease" and "concentration" rather than happiness and one-pointedness. C is the third dhyāna; D the space concentration.

quiz.q: How does the sūtra describe the factor of initial thought?
options: suchness-thought, great thought; deliberation, great deliberation; contemplating the nature of mind
quiz.why: Initial thought is suchness-thought and great thought, deliberation and great deliberation, contemplating the nature of mind. The others describe reflection, joy, and concentration.

quiz.q: How does the sūtra describe the factor of ease?
options: ease of mind, body, and sensation, receiving a blissful touch
quiz.why: Ease is ease of mind, body, and sensation, receiving a blissful touch.

quiz.q: Why does the text say these five factors must be explained separately?
options: they differ vastly from the five factors of other sūtras and treatises
quiz.why: The five factors this sūtra describes differ vastly from those in other sūtras and treatises, so they need a separate explanation.

quiz.q: What is suchness-thought?
options: the preliminary concentration before the first dhyāna, the not-yet-arrived state, which arises only through cultivation
quiz.why: Suchness-thought is the preliminary concentration arising before the first dhyāna, the not-yet-arrived state, realized only through cultivation.

quiz.q: Which of the three is contemplated first, and what does a sharp mind perceive?
options: the breath first; it gathers nowhere entering, scatters nowhere leaving, coming and going by no path, like wind in space
form first; the body is solid
quiz.why: One must first contemplate the breath; a bright mind perceives it gathering nowhere entering and scattering nowhere leaving, like wind in empty space.

quiz.q: In contemplating form as suchness, how is the body said to come about?
options: form is originally nonexistent; past deluded thought draws together the four elements encircling space, provisionally called a body
quiz.why: Form is originally nonexistent; past-life deluded thought draws together the present four elements, whose form encircles space, provisionally called the body.

quiz.q: How is mind as suchness investigated?
options: because of mind there is bodily form; mind arises by conditions, swiftly ceasing, without place or mark, only a name, and the name too is empty
quiz.why: Bodily form exists because of mind; closely contemplated, mind depends on conditions, arises and ceases swiftly, has no dwelling or mark, only a name, and the name too is empty.

quiz.q: What makes it "suchness-thought"?
options: the mind is like a mirror
the practitioner no longer finds the three natures distinct
the mind is still as space
quiz.why: When the practitioner no longer finds the three natures, breath, form, and mind, to be distinct, this is suchness-thought.

quiz.q: Why does not finding the breath mean penetrating form and mind as empty?
options: the three are inseparable; their combination produces everything, so if they are unarisen all dharmas are empty
quiz.why: The three are never separate; their combination gives rise to every aggregate, affliction, and karma, so understanding them as unarisen shows all dharmas empty.

quiz.q: In the realization of suchness-thought, how are desire-realm concentration and the not-yet-arrived state distinguished?
options: mind abiding in suchness, bright and pure, is desire-realm concentration; then corresponding with suchness, no longer seeing the three as distinct, like space, is the not-yet-arrived state
quiz.why: Abiding spontaneously in suchness, bright and pure, is desire-realm concentration; after it, no longer seeing body, breath, and mind as distinct, like space, is suchness-thought, the not-yet-arrived state.
